findings.quoteSource: sicuti est, Ne intres in judicium cum servo tuo, quoniam non justificabitur in conspectu tuo omnis vivens, et caetera talia
findings.quoteTarget: even though he uses free will (such as Do not enter into judgment with your servant, for in your sight no one living will be justified, and other such texts), are to be understood otherwise than they sound
findings.problem: The examples (sicuti est … et caetera talia) illustrate the testimonia Scripturarum, and in Latin the case endings keep that link across the sentence (testimonia … aliter accipienda). In the English the parenthesis stands after “even though he uses free will”, twenty-four words away from its antecedent “the testimonies of the Scriptures”, and the verb of that subject (“are to be understood”) arrives only after it. A reader can attach the examples to “free will” or to “is found without sin” instead of to the testimonies, and the unmarked quotation has no visible end (“and other such texts” can be read as part of it). The sense is intact and the distance exists in the Latin too: this is a readability fault of the English sentence, not a fidelity fault.
findings.proposal: Move the parenthesis up to its antecedent, which also restores the Latin order of “nullum hominem hic viventem, quamvis utatur libero arbitrio, inveniri sine peccato”, and leave the rest of the sentence unchanged: “…that the testimonies of the Scriptures (such as Do not enter into judgment with your servant, for in your sight no one living will be justified, and other such texts), by which, I think, it has been settled that no human being living here, even though he uses free will, is found without sin, are to be understood otherwise than they sound, …”

findings.quoteSource: et in eo utique adjuvat, quod docendo aufert ignorantiam
findings.quoteTarget: and God certainly helps in that, by teaching, he removes ignorance
findings.problem: The Latin is one plain construction, in eo … quod: “he helps in that he removes ignorance”, with docendo as the means. The English folds in eo … quod into “in that” and then puts “by teaching” between “in that” and its clause, with a comma on each side. “In that,” then reads as a demonstrative (“in that respect”) followed by a comma splice (“by teaching, he removes ignorance”), and the reader has to rebuild the construction. The sense survives (God helps by removing ignorance through teaching), but this is the clause that states what the opponents mean by divine help, so it should read cleanly.
findings.proposal: and God certainly helps in that he removes ignorance by teaching, so that a human being may know what he must avoid and what he must seek in his works

summary: No CRITIC or MAJOR finding; verdict ok. Two MINOR findings, both about the readability of the English syntax (par. 2: the scripture examples stand twenty-four words away from the testimonies they illustrate; par. 3: “helps in that, by teaching, he removes ignorance”). No SURSA_POSIBIL_ERONATA. All 8 sentences of the source (3 + 3 + 2) have a counterpart in the English, in the same order, checked in both directions: nothing is missing and nothing is added beyond what English needs (“such a person” after esse, fuisse, fore; “then” before “whoever”; “God” repeated as the subject of adjuvat). Negations and quantifiers (nullum … sine peccato; non justificabitur omnis vivens as “no one living will be justified”; nemo est, aut fuit, aut erit; non multum erratur, nec perniciose; non putet … nisi; nec … audent; non ferenda; non fieri), conditionals (si ab homine impleri potest; si … potuerit … et demonstraverit; si nemo est …; si tamen … nisi), concessives (quamvis … pertineat; quamvis utatur libero arbitrio) and purpose clauses (ut … ostendant; ut sciat; quo … mereatur) are kept. Modality is kept at the author’s strength (fortasse respondeas, non esse credendum, instandum est, resistendum est, existimo, quod magis credo, quantum ego judicare possum, debes … non dubitare). Roles are kept (ab homine impleri: a human being can accomplish it; God creates, teaches and helps; the human being enters the way and deserves to reach the life). The crux qui non ei, non solum minime adversatus, verum etiam plurimum gratulatus fuerit … agitatur (par. 2) was read independently: the only construction that fits non mediocribus invidentiae stimulis is the one in which the outer non negates the whole pair, and “does not both refrain from opposing him in the least and even congratulate him heartily” has that scope and avoids the opposite reading that “does not only refrain … but also congratulate” would invite; the same comma after ei is in the raw OCR text, so it does not come from the cleaning. Also accepted after checking against the Latin: munus as “gift” (it pairs with opus, with Phil. 2:13 and with gratuiti muneris in the next paragraph); pro bona voluntate left open; ad eam tenendo proficere as “make progress by holding a course toward it” (both members of vel … perficere, vel … proficere are kept; the printed text reads tenendo and the raw pages carry no variant note here). Scripture: Phil. 2:13 (Old Latin velle et operari) and Ps. 142:2 (Vulgate numbering; Ps. 143:2 in the Hebrew numbering) are correctly identified and translated as the author’s text; the job has no references (references: []), so there is no target form to compare, and the English has no Latin abbreviations or roman numerals. No names beyond God and the Apostle, no numbers. Terminology follows the glossary and the profile (righteousness, righteously, justified, sin, free will, will, the Apostle, the Scriptures, human being for homo) and is consistent inside the batch (work for opus and operari; help for adiutorium, ops, adiuvare); the draft’s TERMEN_NOU flags are not duplicated. No calque from calques-en.json, no archaism, American spelling, curly apostrophes, no straight quotation marks. translation-check --strict on the draft exits 0 (CRITIC 0, MAJOR 0, MINOR 0, INFO 9, all FLAG_PROPOSED; 383 source words, 571 target words, ratio 1.234); the draft and the check report were not changed. The Latin of the job equals the raw OCR text (content/sources/augustine-de-spiritu-et-littera/raw.txt) for all three paragraphs, except for a running head and the colon after fallitur, an OCR repair documented in SOURCE.md that does not affect the rendering (the proviso si tamen … is “provided, however”). Choices of the draft reviewed and accepted without a finding: hic as “here” (four times in par. 2; par. 1 renders in hac vita as “in this life”, so the author’s two expressions stay distinct), “which I am more inclined to believe” for quod magis credo, “the best, the one by which” for optimum, quo fiat, “free will” absorbing voluntatis, “self-control” for continenter, “commandments” for praecepta, “deserve” for mereatur.
